title: Human Capital Formation in India
summary: Human capital is the stock of skill, knowledge and expertise embodied in the people of a nation. This chapter explains the sources of human capital formation, its role in economic growth, the difference between physical and human capital and between human capital and human development, and the state of education and health in India along with the problems and policies of human capital formation.

notes.heading: Meaning of human capital and human capital formation
notes.html:
Human capital is the stock of skill, ability, expertise, education and knowledge embodied in the people of a nation at a point of time. It is a stock concept.

Human capital formation is the process of adding to the stock of human capital over time, by investing in education, health, training and other means. It is a flow concept. It turns people into productive resources: an engineer or a doctor contributes far more to output than an untrained worker.

Just as a society converts raw materials into productive physical capital (e.g. a factory), it can convert people into productive human capital through investment in them.

notes.heading: Sources of human capital formation
notes.html:
• Expenditure on education: the most important source. Individuals spend on education expecting higher future earnings; governments spend because education also yields social benefits (spreads to others, raises productivity and awareness).
  • Expenditure on health: a healthy person works more efficiently and for more days. Preventive medicine (vaccination), curative medicine (treatment), social medicine (spread of health literacy) and provision of clean drinking water and sanitation are all forms of investment in health.
  • On-the-job training: firms train workers at the workplace under skilled workers or send them for off-campus courses. The firm insists that workers stay for a period so it can recover the cost through higher productivity.
  • Migration: people migrate (rural to urban, or abroad) in search of better jobs. The costs of transport, higher living costs and psychological costs are incurred because enhanced earnings outweigh them. Migration improves the utilisation of skills.
  • Expenditure on information: money spent to obtain information about the labour market (jobs, salaries) and about education and health facilities, which helps people make better decisions about investing in themselves.

notes.heading: Physical capital vs human capital
notes.html:
BasisPhysical capitalHuman capital
TangibilityTangible; can be seen and sold in the marketIntangible; embodied in the person, cannot be sold (only its services)
SeparabilitySeparable from its ownerInseparable from its owner
MobilityCompletely mobile between countries (except buildings)Not perfectly mobile; restricted by nationality and culture
FormationCan be imported; formed through economic and technical decisionsBuilt consciously through education, health and training; largely a social process
DepreciationDepreciates with use and timeDepreciates with ageing but can be offset by continuous investment in education and health
BenefitsMainly private to the ownerPrivate and social benefits (positive externalities)

notes.heading: Human capital and economic growth
notes.html:
• Higher productivity: an educated, healthy worker produces more output per hour; total output (GDP) rises.
  • Innovation and technology: human capital stimulates innovation and creates the ability to absorb and adapt new technologies.
  • Better use of physical capital: machines and technology are only productive when skilled people operate them.
  • Change in attitude: education changes outlook towards modernisation, family size and women's participation.
  • Higher participation: education raises the participation of women and others in productive work.

The relationship runs both ways: higher income makes it possible to spend more on education and health, and better education and health raise income. Empirical evidence shows that both human capital and economic growth have risen together in India, but it is hard to establish exactly which causes which.

India's large stock of skilled workers, especially in information technology, is considered an important factor behind its services-led growth and its role as a knowledge economy.

notes.heading: Human capital vs human development
notes.html:
Human capitalHuman development
Treats education and health as a means to increase labour productivityTreats education and health as ends in themselves, integral to well-being
Investment is worthwhile only if it raises outputEvery person has a right to basic education and health, whatever its effect on output
A narrower conceptA broader concept including freedom, dignity and choices
Human beings as inputs to productionHuman beings as the goal of development

Human development is often measured by the Human Development Index, which combines health (life expectancy), education and per capita income.

notes.heading: Institutions and the role of government
notes.html:
In India, education and health are the responsibility of both the Union and state governments. Government intervention is needed because:

  • education and health services have large social benefits (externalities), so private provision would be too little;
  • private providers may charge high prices, putting services beyond the reach of the poor;
  • individuals often lack full information about the quality and cost of services.
SectorKey institutions
EducationMinistry of Education (renamed from Ministry of Human Resource Development in 2020); NCERT (school curriculum and textbooks); UGC (regulates and funds universities); AICTE (regulates technical education)
HealthMinistry of Health and Family Welfare; Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR)

notes.heading: Education sector in India: growth and policies
notes.html:
• Expenditure: public expenditure on education as a percentage of GDP has risen over the decades but has remained below 6% of GDP, around 4% in recent years. The Kothari Commission (Education Commission, 1964–66) recommended at least 6% of GDP for education, a target reaffirmed by the National Education Policy 2020.
  • Education cess: an education cess on taxes was introduced in 2004; since 2018 a 4% Health and Education cess is levied on income tax to fund these sectors.
  • Right to Education Act, 2009: made free and compulsory education a fundamental right for all children aged 6 to 14 years.
  • Schemes: Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan and later Samagra Shiksha for school education; the mid-day meal scheme (now PM POSHAN) to improve enrolment, attendance and nutrition.
  • National Education Policy 2020: aims at universal access from pre-school to secondary level, a focus on foundational literacy and numeracy, vocational education and a higher gross enrolment ratio in higher education.

Achievements (trend): the literacy rate rose from about 18% in 1951 to about 74% in Census 2011; the gap between male and female literacy has narrowed; elementary enrolment is nearly universal. However, female literacy, quality of learning and access to higher education still lag.

notes.heading: Problems of human capital formation in India
notes.html:
• Rising population: rapid population growth reduces the quality and per capita availability of education and health facilities.
  • Brain drain: migration of highly skilled people such as doctors, engineers and scientists abroad means that the country loses its best human capital, though remittances partly compensate.
  • Insufficient resources: public spending on education and health is below the required level.
  • Deficient manpower planning: mismatch between the skills supplied by the education system and those demanded by the economy, leading to educated unemployment.
  • Low academic standards and quality: lack of trained teachers and infrastructure; emphasis on rote learning.
  • Inequality: gender, rural–urban and regional disparities in access to education and health.
  • Low on-the-job training in the large informal sector, where most workers are engaged.

Way forward: raise public spending towards 6% of GDP, improve quality, expand vocational and skill training (e.g. Skill India), promote girls' education and strengthen primary health care.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is the most important source of human capital formation?
mcqs.explanation: Education raises skill and productivity most directly and has large social benefits, making it the key source.

options: Tangible and separable from its owner
Intangible and inseparable from its owner
Tangible and perfectly mobile across countries
Easily sold in the market like a machine
mcqs.explanation: Skills and knowledge exist within a person, cannot be seen or separated from him, and only their services can be sold.

mcqs.q: The Kothari Commission recommended that public expenditure on education should be at least:
mcqs.explanation: The Education Commission (1964–66) recommended 6% of GDP, a target that has not yet been achieved.

mcqs.q:
Assertion (A): Firms insist that workers stay for a specified period after on-the-job training.
Reason (R): Firms want to recover the cost of training through the higher productivity of trained workers.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: Training is a costly investment by the firm; it can earn a return only if the trained worker continues to work there. R explains A.

mcqs.q: Which body regulates technical education in India?
mcqs.explanation: The All India Council for Technical Education regulates technical education. UGC deals with universities, NCERT with school curriculum and ICMR with medical research.

mcqs.q:
Read the statements:
Statement 1: Human development treats education and health as ends in themselves.
Statement 2: Human capital treats education and health as means to raise labour productivity.
options: Statement 1 is true and Statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false and Statement 2 is true
mcqs.explanation: This is the core distinction: human capital is instrumental, human development is intrinsic.

mcqs.q: The Right to Education Act 2009 provides free and compulsory education to children in the age group:
mcqs.explanation: The RTE Act covers all children from 6 to 14 years of age.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an example of preventive medicine?
mcqs.explanation: Vaccination prevents disease before it occurs. Surgery and antibiotics are curative; health literacy campaigns are social medicine.

options: Loss of memory due to ageing
Migration of unskilled workers from villages to cities
Migration of highly skilled persons to other countries
mcqs.explanation: Brain drain is the loss of a country's best human capital, such as doctors and engineers, through emigration.

mcqs.q: The literacy rate in India as per Census 2011 was about:
mcqs.explanation: Literacy rose from about 18% in 1951 to about 74% in 2011.

mcqs.q: Why is migration considered a source of human capital formation?
options: It raises the population of cities
It reduces the cost of living
It allows people to use their skills in better-paid jobs, raising their productivity and earnings
It always reduces unemployment in the home country
mcqs.explanation: Migrants incur costs because better employment elsewhere lets them put their skills to fuller use, raising earnings.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is not a reason for government intervention in education and health?
options: Private providers may charge high prices
Individuals may lack information about quality
These services have no effect on productivity
mcqs.explanation: Education and health do raise productivity; the other three are genuine reasons for state involvement.

questions.answerHtml: Human capital formation is the process of adding to the stock of human capital over time through investment in education, health, on-the-job training, migration and information.

questions.q: Why is expenditure on information considered a source of human capital formation?
questions.answerHtml: Because information about job markets, salaries and education and health facilities helps people make better decisions about investing in themselves and using their skills efficiently.

questions.q: Distinguish between human capital and human development.
questions.answerHtml:
Human capitalHuman development
Considers education and health as means to increase productivityConsiders education and health as integral to human well-being, i.e. as ends
Investment is justified only if it raises outputBasic education and health are rights of every person regardless of their effect on output
Narrower conceptBroader concept, including freedom and choices

questions.q: Explain on-the-job training and migration as sources of human capital formation.
questions.answerHtml:
On-the-job training: firms train their workers at the workplace, under the supervision of skilled workers, or sponsor them for courses outside. This raises the workers' skill and productivity, and the firm recovers the cost through higher output, which is why it requires trained workers to stay for a certain period.

Migration: people move from rural to urban areas or to other countries for better jobs. Though they incur costs of transport, higher cost of living and psychological costs of living in a strange place, higher earnings in the new place outweigh these. Migration thus leads to fuller and better use of their skills.

questions.q: How does human capital formation contribute to economic growth?
questions.answerHtml:
1. Raises productivity: educated and healthy workers produce more per hour, raising national output.
  2. Promotes innovation: human capital generates new ideas and methods of production and the ability to absorb new technology.
  3. Improves use of physical capital: sophisticated machines and technology need skilled people to operate them; without human capital, physical capital remains underutilised.
  4. Changes attitudes: education promotes modern outlook, smaller families, and greater participation of women in work, all of which support growth.

India's experience in IT and services shows how a skilled workforce can drive growth.

questions.q: 'Brain drain is a major problem of human capital formation in India.' Defend or refute.
questions.answerHtml:
The statement is largely defended.

  • Brain drain is the emigration of highly qualified persons such as doctors, engineers, scientists and IT professionals.
  • The country spends heavily on educating them, often with subsidised public institutions, but the benefits of their skills go to other countries.
  • It creates shortages of skilled personnel in critical areas like health care and research, slowing development.

However, it is partly offset by remittances sent home, transfer of knowledge and networks, and the return of some professionals with experience. Therefore, while it is a real loss, India can reduce it by creating better opportunities and research facilities at home.

questions.q: Distinguish between physical capital and human capital on any six bases.
questions.answerHtml:
BasisPhysical capitalHuman capital
1. NatureTangible: machines, buildingsIntangible: skills, knowledge
2. SeparabilityCan be separated from its ownerCannot be separated from its owner
3. SaleCan be sold in the marketCannot be sold; only its services can be sold
4. MobilityEasily mobile across countries (except buildings)Not perfectly mobile; limited by nationality and culture
5. FormationCan be built through imports and investment decisions of the ownerBuilt through education, health and training; largely a social process
6. DepreciationDepreciates with use and timeDepreciates with age but can be maintained through continuous investment
7. BenefitsMainly privatePrivate and social (positive externalities)

questions.q: Discuss the main problems faced by India in human capital formation and suggest measures to overcome them.
questions.answerHtml:
Problems

  1. Rising population: it puts pressure on schools, colleges and hospitals, lowering per capita availability and quality.
  2. Brain drain: many highly skilled professionals migrate abroad.
  3. Insufficient resources: public spending on education (around 4% of GDP) and health remains below the required levels.
  4. Deficient manpower planning: skills supplied do not match those demanded, leading to educated unemployment.
  5. Low quality: shortage of trained teachers, poor infrastructure and emphasis on rote learning.
  6. Inequalities: large gender, rural–urban and regional gaps in access to education and health.

Measures

  • Raise public expenditure on education towards 6% of GDP and strengthen public health.
  • Improve quality by training teachers and improving infrastructure, as envisaged by NEP 2020.
  • Expand vocational education and skill development linked to job market needs.
  • Promote girls' education and target backward regions.
  • Create better research and job opportunities to retain talent.
